# Face Culling and Visibility Optimization

Also called: Interior Polygon Removal, Removing Interior Polygons

## Overview
Face Culling and Visibility Optimization reduces the rendering load in blocky voxel meshes by reconstructing cubes from triangles and removing sides that are adjacent to solid neighbors, thereby avoiding the rendering of hidden geometry [S1, unofficial]. It solves the problem of naively rendering all six faces of every cube, including those hidden by neighbors, which results in excessive draw calls and vertex processing overhead [S1, unofficial]. Unlike sibling methods that rely on global camera visibility or post-processing opacity thresholds, this family operates primarily on local voxel adjacency to determine face visibility during mesh generation [S1, unofficial].

## Shared principles
The core mechanism involves iterating through occupied voxel positions in a 3D grid and evaluating the occupancy state of immediate neighbors to determine face visibility [Parent]. A face is considered visible if the adjacent voxel in the direction of the face's normal is empty (air/void) or transparent, depending on the specific culling variant [Parent]. If a neighbor exists and is opaque, the shared face is internal and is culled [Parent].

The implementation typically reconstructs cubes from triangles rather than instantiating pre-made models, allowing the engine to determine which sides of a cube should be rendered based on neighbor checks [S1, unofficial]. To optimize performance, the meshes of all individual cubes are often combined into a single big mesh called a 'chunk' [S1, unofficial]. This culling check is performed once during mesh creation, resulting in no framerate loss during rendering [S1, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### [Face Coverage Mask Culling](3397-face-coverage-mask-culling.md)
Face Coverage Mask Culling removes hidden faces of partial voxel shapes (such as stairs or slabs) by representing face coverage as a 16-bit bit mask. It sets itself apart from sibling methods that rely on coarse block visibility by operating at the sub-face granularity, allowing precise culling of geometry that is occluded by neighbors while preserving exposed portions of the same face.

### [ChunkMesh Vertex Packing and Management](3566-chunkmesh-vertex-packing-and-management.md)
ChunkMesh Vertex Packing and Management minimizes GPU memory bandwidth and buffer upload overhead by packing vertex attributes into two 32-bit unsigned integers per vertex. It sets itself apart from sibling culling methods by focusing on the data structure and memory management of the resulting mesh rather than just the visibility determination logic, building on [Face Culling and Visibility Optimization](3861-face-culling-and-visibility-optimization.md).

### [Voxel Backface Culling and Internal Face Masking](4569-voxel-backface-culling-and-internal-face-masking.md)
Voxel Backface Culling and Internal Face Masking rejects invisible faces in voxel rendering by determining front/back orientation in projection space and masking faces shared between neighboring voxels. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like [Face Coverage Mask Culling](3397-face-coverage-mask-culling.md) by operating directly on the geometry shader stage using projection-space dot products and bit-packed visibility codes, rather than pre-computing coverage masks or relying solely on neighbor occupancy checks during mesh generation.

### [Block Visibility Culling](5334-block-visibility-culling.md)
Block Visibility Culling determines which voxel blocks require mesh updates or rendering based on the camera's position and rotation, avoiding unnecessary geometry generation when the viewing direction has not changed significantly. Unlike its sibling [Face Culling](8735-face-culling.md), which relies on local voxel adjacency to hide internal faces, this method operates at the coarse block level by comparing the current camera state against the previous frame's state to skip redundant processing. It further refines visibility by calculating screen-space orientation relative to the player to cull faces that are geometrically facing away from the viewer.

### [Extraction of Surface Points (Sobierajski)](5721-extraction-of-surface-points-sobierajski.md)
Extraction of Surface Points (Sobierajski) is a fast display method for the direct rendering of boundary surfaces by extracting only visible boundary voxels from volume data. It solves the problem of efficiently generating a surface representation for volume rendering by filtering out occluded geometry before the rendering stage. Unlike sibling methods that rely on block-level culling or mesh topology optimization [Face Culling and Visibility Optimization](3861-face-culling-and-visibility-optimization.md), this method operates on individual voxel boundaries and uses orthographic projection visibility to prune the voxel list, making it suitable for real-time previewing and interactive manipulation.

### [Mask Projection Culling](6836-mask-projection-culling.md)
Mask Projection Culling is a visibility optimization technique that filters mesh vertices and faces by projecting them into multiple camera views and checking if they fall within dilated binary masks, removing geometry not visible in any view. Unlike local adjacency-based methods like [Face Culling](8735-face-culling.md) or [Block Visibility Culling](5334-block-visibility-culling.md) which rely on voxel occupancy, this method uses global camera visibility to cull geometry, making it suitable for sparse or non-voxel-based representations where view-dependent occlusion is significant. It sets itself apart from [Face Coverage Mask Culling](3397-face-coverage-mask-culling.md) by operating on the final mesh geometry rather than pre-computed face coverage data, and from [Mesh Culling via 3D Projection and Connected Components](6963-mesh-culling-via-3d-projection-and-connected-components.md) by relying on binary mask intersection rather than connected component analysis.

### [Mesh Culling via 3D Projection and Connected Components](6963-mesh-culling-via-3d-projection-and-connected-components.md)
This method culls mesh geometry by projecting vertices into multiple camera views and comparing their depths against reference depth maps to identify and remove unseen or forecast geometry. It sets itself apart from local adjacency-based culling (like [Face Culling](8735-face-culling.md)) by using global visibility information from arbitrary camera poses, making it suitable for unbounded reconstructions where local neighbor checks fail to detect distant occlusions or artifacts.

### [Face Culling](8735-face-culling.md)
Face Culling is a mesh generation optimization that reduces the number of vertices and triangles sent to the GPU by skipping the rendering of voxel faces that are adjacent to existing neighboring voxels. It solves the problem of naively rendering all six faces of every cube, including those hidden by neighbors, which results in excessive draw calls and vertex processing overhead. Unlike [Block Visibility Culling](5334-block-visibility-visibility-culling.md) which operates at a higher level, Face Culling operates at the individual face level within a block, ensuring that only exposed surfaces contribute to the final mesh.

### [Opacity-based Mesh Culling](8759-opacity-based-mesh-culling.md)
Opacity-based Mesh Culling is a post-processing technique applied to polygonal meshes extracted from volumetric or neural representations to reduce geometric complexity. It solves the problem of excessive mesh density by discarding triangles that contribute negligible visual information, specifically those with low cumulative opacity. Unlike sibling methods that rely on spatial adjacency or block occupancy [Face Culling and Visibility Optimization](3861-face-culling-and-visibility-optimization.md), this method evaluates the intrinsic radiometric properties of individual faces. It sets itself apart by directly linking mesh retention to the alpha channel (opacity) of the source representation, often achieving drastic reductions in triangle count (e.g., down to 5% of the original) while preserving visual fidelity.

### [From-Region Visibility Preprocessing](9048-from-region-visibility-preprocessing.md)
From-region visibility preprocessing is a technique that precomputes the visibility of geometric regions (such as clusters of triangles or voxels) from specific viewpoints or regions of interest to optimize rendering performance. It solves the problem of expensive per-frame visibility determination by shifting the computational burden to an offline or semi-offline phase. Unlike parent methods that rely on local voxel adjacency for face culling, this approach handles complex, non-axis-aligned geometry and occluder fusion, distinguishing it from simpler block-based culling.

### Buried Bitmask Optimization
A bitmask used to track which blocks in a chunk are 'buried' (fully surrounded by opaque blocks), allowing the renderer to skip mesh generation for those blocks [S2, unofficial]. The algorithm resets the buried bitmask for the chunk, creates `MappedAdjacentChunks` for the current chunk position to access neighboring chunks, and iterates through all blocks in the chunk (0 to `CHUNK_SIZE`) to determine if each is buried by calling `block->isBuried(...)` and setting the corresponding flag in the bitmask [S2, unofficial]. If all blocks in the chunk are buried (checked via `buriedBitmask->AreAllBlocksSet()`), the mesh is marked as empty and mesh generation is skipped [S2, unofficial]. When generating the mesh, any block that is air or has its buried flag set in the bitmask is skipped [S2, unofficial].

### Two-pass transparent meshing with opaque separation
A meshing strategy that separates opaque and transparent geometry into two passes to ensure correct rendering order and reduce overdraw, by generating opaque faces between air/transparent blocks and transparent faces only for blocks touching air [S3, unofficial]. The first pass (opaque) generates faces for opaque blocks; if the chunk contains transparent blocks, it tests for opaque blocks (ignoring transparent and air) to generate opaque faces between air and transparent blocks, otherwise it tests for non-air blocks [S3, unofficial]. The second pass (transparent) tests for non-air blocks to mark only transparent blocks, generating faces for all transparent blocks touching air but not adding faces between transparent and solid blocks [S3, unofficial]. Solid block types are filtered out during the transparent pass by checking if the block type is not transparent before constructing the AO value and adding the block type to the hashmap [S3, unofficial].

## Background
The concept of removing interior polygons to improve rendering performance originated in the context of voxel-based procedural terrain generation, specifically referencing implementations similar to Minecraft [S1, unofficial]. The initial observation was that brute-force instantiation of cube models resulted in the engine needlessly rendering 12 triangles (6 sides) when only 2 triangles (1 side) were visible, leading to the optimization of reconstructing cubes from triangles and removing sides adjacent to solid neighbors [S1, unofficial]. This approach was further optimized by combining the meshes of all cubes into a single big mesh called a 'chunk' [S1, unofficial].
